title: `.progress` named list errors on elements that are not cli progress bar arguments
description:
Downstream report: tidyverse/purrr#1253 (fix proposed in tidyverse/purrr#1282).

When `.progress` is supplied as a named list to `collect_mirai()`, the list is spliced verbatim into `cli::cli_progress_bar()` via `do.call()`. Any element that is not a formal argument of `cli::cli_progress_bar()` causes collection to error. purrr's `.progress` specification injects such an element (`caller`) via `as_progress()`, so a named-list `.progress` fails when purrr runs in parallel with mirai daemons set:

```r
library(mirai)

daemons(sync = TRUE)
m <- mirai_map(1:2, identity)
collect_mirai(m, list(.progress = list(name = "test", caller = environment())))
#> Error: unused argument (caller = <environment>)
daemons(0)
```

There is also a latent mirai-only variant: an element duplicating an argument mirai passes itself errors differently:

```r
collect_mirai(m, list(.progress = list(total = 100L)))
#> Error: formal argument "total" matched by multiple actual arguments
```

Fix: filter list elements against `names(formals(cli::cli_progress_bar))`, excluding `total`, `current`, `auto_terminate` and `.envir` which mirai sets itself, so non-matching elements are ignored. Implemented in b80ba14 on branch `progress-list-args`.

title: Scoping bug for mirai map progress bars
Allow .progress to accept an already-created cli progress bar
description:
🤖 Written by AI 🤖

`collect_mirai()` accepts `.progress` in `options`, but it always creates its own cli progress bar with a total equal to the number of mirai being collected.

Would you consider also allowing `.progress` to accept an already-created progress bar (e.g. a cli bar id or bar object), which `collect_mirai()` would then tick once per collected mirai instead of creating and closing its own bar?

Motivating use case: in purrr, `map_if()` evaluates a predicate map and a transformation map as two separate phases, and we'd like a single progress bar spanning both phases (total = 2n). We now do this for sequential maps by creating the bar on the R side and ticking it directly from purrr's C loop, but a parallelized predicate goes through `mirai_map()` + `collect_mirai()`, which can only show its own separate bar. If `collect_mirai()` could tick a caller-provided bar, parallel phases could participate in the same shared progress bar as sequential ones.

Related: https://github.com/r-lib/cli/issues/850 (cli providing an official way to pass an R-created bar to C code).

title: Question about memory explosion in my R package
description:
Hi @shikokuchuo,

I have used `mirai` in my R package,`orthanc`, to be able to perform API requests/queries in parallel but I am noticing an issue of the memory use exploding when running in parallel (i.e., setting `mirai::daemons()` versus a main process sequential run.

`mirai` is used by way of `purrr::in_parallel()` inside a `purrr::map()`. So when `daemons()` is not set, it performs the map sequential in the main process and, for this example I'm running right this second, the memory is very low (~1GB, lets say) according to the Positron memory profiler. However, when I set `daemons()` and it runs in separate child processes, the main process shoots up to 60+ GB of memory (even though each child process doing the actual work is seemingly low footprint).

I don't know if you have a suggestion for how I can profile this better to find out where the memory issue is happening in my code. I can't understand why this would happen.

The code for this parallelized function is here, for what that's worth: https://github.com/mattwarkentin/orthanc/blob/main/R/filtering.R

The job of the function is fairly straightforward. We have a list of objects (`Patients`) and we loop over them (potentially in parallel) to apply predicate functions to remove certain patients/studies/series/instances that do not meet the logical condition.

Here is some example code:
```r
library(orthanc)
library(mirai)

client <- Orthanc$new("https://orthanc.uclouvain.be/demo")

# Sequential, in-process
find_and_filter_patients(
  client = client,
  instance_filter = \(x) {
    x$frames == 1L
  }
)

# Asynchronous, child-processes
daemons(4)
find_and_filter_patients(
  client = client,
  instance_filter = \(x) {
    x$frames == 1L
  }
)
```

Any guidance would be greatly appreciated!

title: as.promise.mirai(): a mirai that completes between unresolved() and .keep() never resolves its promise
description:
mirai 2.7.3, nanonext 1.10.3, promises 1.5.0, later 1.4.8, R 4.6 on macOS arm64.

`as.promise.mirai()` does:

```r
promises::promise(function(resolve, reject) {
  if (unresolved(x)) .keep(x, environment()) else resolve(.subset2(x, "value"))
})
```

`rnng_set_promise_context()` only stores the callback pointer. If the aio
completed after `unresolved()` returned `TRUE` and before the pointer was set,
`raio_complete()` found `cb == NULL` and never scheduled the `later` call, and
nothing checks for completion when the context is set. The promise stays
pending forever.

### Deterministic reproduction, forcing the window

```r
mirai::daemons(1, dispatcher = TRUE)
invisible(mirai::mirai(1)[])
keep <- get(".keep", asNamespace("mirai"))
for (gap in c(0, 0.2)) {
  m <- mirai::mirai(1)
  p <- promises::promise(function(resolve, reject) {
    if (mirai::unresolved(m)) { Sys.sleep(gap); keep(m, environment()) } else resolve(m$data)
  })
  start <- Sys.time()
  while (attr(p, "promise_impl")$status() == "pending" && difftime(Sys.time(), start, units = "secs") < 2) later::run_now(0.02)
  cat(sprintf("gap=%.1f unresolved=%s promise=%s\n", gap, mirai::unresolved(m), attr(p, "promise_impl")$status()))
}
mirai::daemons(0)
#> gap=0.0 unresolved=FALSE promise=fulfilled
#> gap=0.2 unresolved=FALSE promise=pending
```

### How it happens in practice

The first `.keep()` in a process loads `later` (measured at 26 ms against 0 ms
for later calls), which is long enough for a trivial task to complete. In the
chain below the first mirai has resolved by the time `then()` is called and
takes the `resolve()` branch, so the second mirai is the first to call
`.keep()` (verified by wrapping `.keep` to record its callers: only `m2`
appears), and its completion lands during the load. Run as a fresh process:

```r
mirai::daemons(2, dispatcher = TRUE)
done <- FALSE; m2 <- NULL
shiny::testServer(function(input, output, session) {
  shiny::observe({
    m1 <- mirai::mirai(1)
    promises::then(m1, function(v) {
      m2 <<- mirai::mirai(2)
      promises::then(m2, function(v) done <<- TRUE)
    })
  })
}, {
  session$flushReact()
  start <- Sys.time()
  while (!done && difftime(Sys.time(), start, units = "secs") < 3) { session$flushReact(); later::run_now(0.02) }
  cat(sprintf("done=%s m2 unresolved=%s promise=%s\n", done, mirai::unresolved(m2), attr(m2$promise, "promise_impl")$status()))
})
mirai::daemons(0)
#> done=FALSE m2 unresolved=FALSE promise=pending
```

Run a second time in the same process it succeeds.

### Suggested fix

After `.keep()`, check `unresolved(x)` once more and call `resolve()` if the
aio has completed, or have `rnng_set_promise_context()` schedule the callback
itself when `raio->result` is already set.

title: A throwing unserialization hook (`ufunc`) crashes the daemon and hangs all subsequent tasks
description:
If a `ufunc` registered via `register_serial()` / `serial_config()` throws, the error propagates out of R's `unserialize()` refhook and the daemon process aborts (`Execution halted`). The dispatcher then waits for the dead daemon, and **every subsequent task hangs indefinitely**.

Reproducible example:

```r
library(mirai)

cfg <- serial_config(
  "cvhandle",
  sfunc = list(function(o) serialize(NULL, NULL)),
  ufunc = list(function(r) stop("hook failure"))
)
daemons(1, serial = cfg)

# external pointer -> actually hits the refhook
obj <- structure(nanonext::cv(), class = "cvhandle")

m1 <- mirai(TRUE, x = obj)
m1[]          # -> errorValue (daemon has already crashed)

m2 <- mirai(1 + 1)
m2[]          # hangs forever
```

**Expected:** a throwing `ufunc` should surface as an `errorValue` for that task, and the daemon should remain usable (or restart cleanly) for later tasks.

**Workaround** (what we're doing in r-polars): wrap each `ufunc` so it returns the condition instead of throwing. `ufunc = function(x) tryCatch(deserialize(x), error = function(e) e)`.

**Environment:** mirai 2.7.2, nanonext 1.10.2, R 4.6.1, Linux.

Found in pola-rs/r-polars#1842

title: Feature Request: Support Functional Lazy Generators in `mirai()` to Prevent Memory Explosion
description:
### Problem

When queuing thousands of rolling-window tasks (e.g., from `rsample`), individual splits are extremely lightweight because R's lexical scoping allows closure environments to share references to the same parent dataframe via pointers without duplication.

However, `mirai()` currently enforces **Eager Serialization** on the main thread before pushing messages into the NNG queue. This breaks R's reference-sharing mechanism, causing the parent dataframe to be duplicated inside the binary payload of *every single task*. A 10MB dataframe with 100 splits instantly balloons into 1GB of binary junk in the NNG buffer, leading to immediate Out-of-Memory (OOM) crashes.

### Proposal

Could `mirai()` support a **Functional Lazy Generator** mechanism to defer both evaluation and serialization until the exact moment a task is dispatched?

Instead of passing evaluated R objects or standard expressions, `mirai()` could accept a lightweight R closure (a generator function).

1. **At Queue Time:** The main thread only stores the `SEXP` pointer of the closure in an R-level queue (protected from GC via `PROTECT`). Memory footprint remains virtually zero.
2. **At Dispatch Time:** Only when an NNG channel signals it is ready to push a message to an available worker, the main thread triggers the closure, evaluates the data slice on-the-fly, and serializes the return value directly into the stream.

**Conceptual API:**

```R
# Current Eager Way (Causes Memory Explosion):
# purrr::map(all_splits, \(s) mirai(run_backtest(s)))

# Proposed Pure Lazy Closure Way:
purrr::map(all_splits, \(s) {
  # Create a zero-argument closure that locks 's' via reference scoping
  lazy_task <- function() run_backtest(s)
  
  # mirai stores the closure pointer and only invokes/serializes it on-demand
  mirai(.lazy_closure = lazy_task)
})

```

By postponing serialization to the last millisecond before transmission, `mirai` could maintain its blazing-fast asynchronous I/O while scaling to massive backtesting datasets without any application-level chunking workarounds.

title: Uninformative errors from mirai_map() collection for non-mirai errorValues
description:
When `.stop` or `.flat` collection encounters a task that resolved to a plain 'errorValue' — cancelled (20), timed out (5), or a crashed daemon (19) — `stop_m()` reads a `message` attribute that only a 'miraiError' carries. With cli, the raised error is a bare "In index: 1." with a message-less parent condition, giving no indication of what went wrong. Without cli, `sprintf()` with the NULL attribute yields `character(0)` and the error is raised with a completely empty message. A 'miraiInterrupt' takes the same path.

```r
library(mirai)
daemons(1)
mp <- mirai_map(30, Sys.sleep)
stop_mirai(mp)
mp[.stop]
#> Error in `mirai_map()`:
#> i In index: 1.
# no cause reported - and an empty message entirely without cli
daemons(0)
```

The fix derives the message by error kind: the message attribute for a 'miraiError' as now, `nng_error()` for integer 'errorValue's, and "Interrupted" for a 'miraiInterrupt', with a proper `errorCondition()` parent in the cli branch.

title: mirai_map() collection option .flat ignores an errorValue in the first element
description:
The `.flat` collection option only checks `is_error_value()` for elements from index 2 onwards. As a result, a single-element map that fails returns the miraiError as the flattened value with no error raised at all, and a failure in the first element of a longer map surfaces as a misleading "cannot flatten outputs of differing type" error instead of the underlying condition.

```r
library(mirai)
daemons(1)
mirai_map(list("a"), function(x) x + 1L)[.flat]
#> returns the miraiError silently as the result

tryCatch(mirai_map(list("a", 2L), function(x) x + 1L)[.flat], error = conditionMessage)
#> "cannot flatten outputs of differing type: character / double"
daemons(0)
```

The fix hoists the error check so it applies to every collected element, consistent with `.stop` and with the documented behaviour that `.flat` "errors if an 'errorValue' has been returned".

title: daemon() returns exit code 1 (idletime) when walltime elapses while idle
description:
A daemon whose `walltime` elapses while idle exits with code 1 ("idletime limit reached") rather than 2 ("walltime limit reached"), even when `idletime` was never set. The recv timeout is capped at `min(idletime, walltime)`, but a timed-out recv is always attributed to idletime.

```r
sock <- nanonext::socket("req", listen = url <- mirai::local_url())
xc <- mirai::daemon(url, dispatcher = FALSE, autoexit = FALSE, walltime = 500)
mirai::nextcode(xc)
#> "1 | Daemon idletime limit reached"  # should be 2 | walltime
close(sock)
```

The walltime code 2 is currently only returned if a task happens to arrive after the deadline. This matters for launcher packages that key respawn decisions off the exit codes translated by `nextcode()`. The fix is to attribute a recv timeout to walltime when the walltime deadline has passed, mirroring the existing precedence where the higher code wins when multiple limits are exceeded.

title: race_mirai() returns 0 without waiting for profiles set with url and dispatcher = FALSE
description:
For compute profiles created with `daemons(url = , dispatcher = FALSE)`, `race_mirai()` returns `0L` immediately while tasks are still unresolved. `0L` is documented to mean the list is empty, so the documented pattern `remaining[[idx]]` errors.

```r
library(mirai)
daemons(url = local_url(), dispatcher = FALSE)
launch_local(1)
Sys.sleep(1)
m <- mirai({ Sys.sleep(0.3); "done" })
race_mirai(list(m))  # 0 immediately - should wait and return 1
```

The cause is that `create_sock()` is the one profile constructor that does not set a `cv` on the profile environment (`launch_daemons()` and dispatcher profiles both do), and `race_aio()` with a NULL cv degrades silently to `0L` rather than erroring. The fix is to create the cv in `create_sock()`, making it a true profile invariant. This also makes `race_mirai()` work for synchronous compute profiles, which share this path.

title: Daemon crashes if an error is raised before evaluation begins
description:
If a task errors before the `eval()` frame exists — for instance when assigning `...` globals into the daemon's global environment fails — `mk_mirai_error()` finds no eval frame on the stack, `max(which(...))` returns `-Inf`, and the subscript that follows throws from inside the error handler. The secondary error escapes `daemon()` and takes down the daemon process: the host receives an errorValue 19 (connection reset) instead of a miraiError, and the daemon is not replaced.

Repro:

```r
library(mirai)
daemons(1, dispatcher = FALSE)
everywhere({ assign("x", 1, envir = globalenv()); lockBinding("x", globalenv()) })[]
m <- mirai(x + 1, x = 2)
m[]                          # errorValue 19, should be miraiError
info()[["connections"]]     # 0 - daemon gone
```

The fix is to only trim and attach the stack trace when the eval frame is actually found, so pre-eval errors return a regular miraiError (message intact, no stack trace) and the daemon survives.

title: `cleanup = TRUE` does not restore options modified by evaluated code
description:
When a daemon starts, it takes a snapshot of the session state so that `cleanup = TRUE` can restore it after each task. For options, the snapshot stored `.Options`.

However `.Options` is not a copy — it is the live options object itself, which `options()` modifies in place. The saved "snapshot" therefore silently tracks every subsequent change, and the restore step just re-applies whatever the options currently are. The result is that any option set by a mirai task persists for all later tasks on that daemon, despite `cleanup = TRUE`:

```r
library(mirai)
daemons(1)
mirai(options(digits = 3))[]
mirai(getOption("digits"))[]
#> [1] 3   # expected 7
daemons(0)
```

The fix is to snapshot a real copy with `as.list(.Options)`, which adds only ~1µs at daemon startup.

title: Signal mechanism from daemon to host
description:
> _(This message has been a journey.)_
> 
> After more research, I cannot find a specific "signal" mechanism so that the R expression can immediately be signaled back to the main host while the rest of the expression continues to execute.
> 
> Long-story-short, I enabled `daemons(..., output=TRUE)` to see errors/warnings immediately, nice that they are passed immediately. I thought they may be passed back to the local process as `"condition"`s in which case handlers would be able to work on them, but alas I believe they are being merely `cat`'ed (or equivalent) to the local console.
> 
> From this, two questions:
> 
> - Is it possible to tag the remote-output with a particular `"condition"` where its default local handler is merely `cat(cond)`? This would continue the current behavior, but would allow a calling handler to deal with remote output distinctly from local output. (If always doing this as a condition is concerning, it could be as an option, something like `daemons(.., output=T, output_condition=T)`.)
> - I see the [since-removed](https://github.com/r-lib/mirai/commit/77ca46aad07dbc871345429db4be0e3df69aa906) `.signal=` argument which references `nanonext::cv()`, is `cv()` applicable here? Is there a way to allow remote signals (distinct from console output) to be caught via the normal R mechanisms?
> 
> I'm adding this comment mostly to say that I continue to look into the source to hope to self-answer, but I'm not finding something to lead me to a working solution. Since this discussion has spiraled from `unassigned()` to a bit more, would it be better as a Discussion?

title: Feature Request: Expose headers as a customizable component of `http_config`
description:
Hi there! I'm toying around with some `mirai` utilities for Domino and ran into a bit of a hurdle with `http_config` -- this function seems to be the perfect entry point for us to provision compute, but I ran into one rather annoying hurdle.

### Root cause

Currently, the headers for the http requests are fixed and rather specific to the default api endpoint:

https://github.com/r-lib/mirai/blob/bad3380db943455a839dbefc192142b9c5ef0f73/R/launchers.R#L555-L559

### Workaround

I've come up with an absolutely horrible hack that lets me trick `mirai` into accepting my own headers by using the `data` function to mutate the parent environment, such that headers gets set as an active binding that disallows mutation. This workaround is really messy and error-prone.

```r
# simplified example to focus only on the header injection
data <- function(...) {
  my_headers <- c("Content-Type" = "application/json")
  makeActiveBinding("headers", function(...) my_headers, sys.frame(-2L))
  '{ "cmd": "%s" }'
}
```

### Suggested Changes

Given that pretty much every other part of the request is customizable, this seems like it was just an oversight. However, adding a `headers` parameter might draw into question the explicit `http_config` `token` and `cookie` parameters which might be better served by a generic `headers` parameter.

For backwards compatibility, the parameter redundancy could be addressed like this:

```r
http_config <- function(
  url = posit_workbench_url,
  method = "POST",
  cookie = posit_workbench_cookie,
  token = NULL,
  data = posit_workbench_data,

  # derive headers in the function signature based on provided cookie and token
  headers = posit_workbench_headers(token, cookie),  

  ...
)
```

title: Switch `capacity` from task count to memory budget (MB)
description:
The `capacity` argument added in #454 caps `dispatcher inflight = queued + executing` as an integer task count. A count is a poor proxy for the resource we actually want to bound — host memory:

- 1 task with a 500 MB global and 10,000 tasks with 50 KB globals look identical to the gate.
- Executing tasks no longer hold memory host-side (the `nng_msg` is consumed on `nng_sendmsg`), so counting them inflates perceived pressure.

Since dispatcher is now a thread inside the host process (#581), the inq linked list of queued `nng_msg` lives in host RAM. That is the resource at risk of OOM, and it is denominated in bytes.

**Change:**
- `capacity` becomes a memory budget in MB (metric — 1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes) over queued task payloads.
- `NULL` (default) remains unbounded; degenerate values (0, non-finite, negative) degrade to unbounded.
- New `dispatcher_capacity()` accessor returns `c(used, peak, capacity)` in MB for monitoring queue pressure.
- Gate skipped entirely on the hot path when `capacity = NULL`, so the default pays no per-task cost.

title: ssh_config() drops username from SSH URLs
description:
## Description

`ssh_config()` ignores the `userinfo` component of SSH URLs. A URL like `ssh://user@192.168.0.101` produces an SSH command targeting `192.168.0.101` instead of `user@192.168.0.101`, so the username is never passed to `ssh`.

## Reproduction

```r
ssh_config("ssh://user@192.168.0.101")$args[[1L]][2L]
#> [1] "192.168.0.101"
# Expected: "user@192.168.0.101"
```

## Cause

`ssh_config()` calls `nanonext::parse_url()` which correctly parses the `userinfo` field, but only the `hostname` and `port` fields are extracted.

## Fix

Include the `userinfo` when constructing the SSH target hostname.

title: Gating dispatcher based on uncollected results
description:
### Problem

`mirai` launches tasks eagerly. If result consumers are slower than producers, results accumulate in memory with no backpressure.

### Proposal

Add a dispatcher option to gate new task launches until a configurable number of results have been collected.

Sketch:

```r
daemons(dispatcher = TRUE, max_uncollected = 10)
```

Usage example:

```r
mirai::daemons(10, dispatcher = TRUE, max_uncollected = 10)

ps <- lapply(1:20, function(x) {
  mirai::mirai({
    # fast background producer
    lock <- filelock::lock("test.log")
    cat(as.character(Sys.time()), "\n", file = "test.log", append = TRUE)
    filelock::unlock(lock)
  }) |> 
    promises::then(function(x) {
      # slow main-thread consumer
      Sys.sleep(2)
    })
})

p <- promises::promise_all(.list = ps)
```

Workers are blocked once `max_uncollected` results are waiting to be collected in the main process. New tasks are dispatched only after the main thread consumes items.

### Benefits

* Prevents unbounded memory growth.
* Removes need for implementing a manual queue.
* Matches `channel(maxsize)` semantics common in other systems.

### Example Use Cases

* **ML dataloader**: avoid preloading large batches faster than they can be consumed by the model.
* **DB write operations**: prevent results from piling up while waiting on a single-threaded writer.

### References

* [mirai#448](https://github.com/r-lib/mirai/issues/448#issuecomment-3323491521)
* [rstudio/promises#142](https://github.com/rstudio/promises/issues/142)
* https://github.com/tidyverse/ragnar/pull/133

description:
mirai today works very well on HPC clusters when run on a login/submit node. Many improvements have been made over the last year or so to make this very user-friendly. Thanks to NNG, the scalability of computations is absolutely amazing ! 

In some cases however users would like to use a standalone server (say Posit Connect or a Shiny Server) to offload some computations onto a HPC cluster. One obvious way how this can be achieved is to make the Connect/Shiny server a submit node of the HPC cluster. Due to security implications this approach is not always desirable let alone allowed - ssh connections on the other hand are a classic and secure way of accessing an HPC cluster. Manual scripting of such an ssh ==> mirai@HPC approach may be feasible but definitely not for the faint-hearted. 

It would be great to get a feature similar to what `clustermq` offers, the ability to transparently allow ssh and slurm to coexist within the framework and with little to no configuration need by a data scientist (cf. https://github.com/sol-eng/Workbench-HPC-Webinar/tree/main/remote-clustermq) 

Happy to be an early tester of such a feature.

title: handling unexpected child exit
description:
If a child node has exited (for whatever reason), I don't see a way to automatically detect this without polling, nor recover gracefully if detected.

For example, detecting appears to require polling.

```r
daemons(4)
everywhere(Sys.getpid())[]
# [[1]]
# [1] 69423
# [[2]]
# [1] 69433
# [[3]]
# [1] 69443
# [[4]]
# [1] 69456
m <- mirai(q('no')) # or some condition causing a crash
unresolved(m)
# [1] FALSE
m[]
# 'errorValue' int 19 | Connection reset
mirai::info()
# connections  cumulative    awaiting   executing   completed 
#           3           4           0           0           6 
```

It's not difficult to infer that we lost one of the nodes (based on `["connections"]`) via polling. Doing this is not onerous from the main node, but it'd be nice if there were other ways such as callbacks or self-detecting.

Once we know that one or more of the children are missing, how do we gracefully recover without killing all of the existing connections? If I call `daemons(4)` again, all of the existing PIDs change (I'm not certain if it's a SIGINT stop, a graceful stop when tasks are complete, or something else).

```r
daemons(4)
everywhere(Sys.getpid())[] # all different
# [[1]]
# [1] 69514
# [[2]]
# [1] 69524
# [[3]]
# [1] 69534
# [[4]]
# [1] 69547
```

Two thoughts on this, knowing they are not trivial:

1. When the current state does not match the intended state (4 connections), what is the best way to repair that state without killing all existing connections? Is there something like `.restart = TRUE` or `.restart="always"`? This gets into interesting (dangerous) territory due to restart limits and other things that other systems address, such as "too many restarts" or rapid restarts; implementation examples include docker and systemd.
2. Can we get callback functionality so that when this condition occurs, we can know something happened instead of having to poll for it? Is there a child-to-parent signal that can be detected? (I'd think polling would not be desired for several reasons.) This might be the first step to be able to support number 1 above.
I'm fine with polling if strictly required, but the graceful respawn of missing connections is difficult to work through.

title: FR: "unassigned()"
description:
Is it possible to determine which tasks (perhaps from `mirai_map()`) have yet to be assigned to a child node?

We have the `unresolved()` helper function that very quickly gives us tasks that have been queued, but there's no indication of whether it has been sent out yet. For instance, if we don't know we have missing children (e.g., https://github.com/r-lib/mirai/issues/539), I do not know how to detect that the tasklist may not be progressing.

Contrived example:

```r
daemons(4)
# simulate the eventual decline due to some problems
everywhere(q('no'))
m <- mirai(1+1)

unresolved(m)
# [1] TRUE
### ... and it never will be resolved
```

title: add `.expr=` arg to `launch_*()`
description:
Stemming from #539, if we add one or more connections, it would be good to be able to run a starting expression on them before they are passed new tasks.

Consider this:

```r
daemons(4, idletime=300)
everywhere(library(dplyr))
# oops, I really need more connections
launch_local(4)
```

In the current state, some have `dplyr` loaded and some do not. In this case it is trivial to call `everywhere(library(dplyr))` again, but it's not hard to imagine either due to time, bandwidth/serialization, or some other reason that we would not want to re-`everything()` to all connections, just to the new connections.

Options:

- `launch_*(.expr=)` so that the new connections are established and the `.expr`ession is executed immediately
- add the ability to subset the connections somehow, which requires both (a) ability to request the "id" (or whatever) of each connection, and (b) pass the list of ids to `everywhere()`

As a hack, if I were using `ssh_config()`, perhaps I might play around with `rscript=` so that it loads R with an initial expression. Not sure if that would actually work, but ... I'm not currently using `ssh_config()`.

What is an ephemeral daemon and is it possible they are still being created by the hundred in my case and using up all the memory?

title: Feature request: add a "disconnected" counter (or equivalent) to status()
description:
@shikokuchuo, I thought of a simplified auto-scaling algorithm for `crew`: https://github.com/wlandau/crew/issues/232. I think it will be powerful. The main advantages are:

1. `crew` will no longer need `mirai::status()$events`.
2. Due to (1), users will safely be able to call `status()` on a `crew` compute profile, supporting interoperability (https://github.com/wlandau/crew/issues/225).
3. `crew` will be better able to adopt the threaded dispatcher when it becomes available in `mirai`.
4. It will position `crew` to better support job arrays (https://github.com/wlandau/crew.cluster/discussions/56).

`mirai` has almost everything I need to implement https://github.com/wlandau/crew/issues/232#issuecomment-32187154542. It just needs one more thing: a cumulative count of the number of worker disconnect events in the current compute profile. Ideally, this count would start at 0 on `mirai::daemons(.compute = "my_compute")`, then increment by 1 every time a worker disconnects for any reason (whether the max idle time is reached, a network error severs the connection, etc.), and never decrement.

Alternatively, a counter of *connection* events would solve the problem equally well (a counter that starts at 0, increments by 1 every time a daemon connects to the compute profile, and does not decrement on disconnect). Just mentioning in case this is easier to track.

Sorry my comments have been all over the place lately. I'll try to stay more organized going forward.

I’ve had a painful little while working out that to get reproducible results, `set.seed()` needs to be called before initialising `daemons()`. The only relevant documentation I found was [this FAQ](https://mirai.r-lib.org/articles/v06-questions.html?q=random#setting-the-random-seed), which got me on the right track after careful study. But I would’ve found it very helpful if it included an example of what it is that you’re supposed to do.

My search also lead me to \#290 and \#324, but I was left puzzled about what the problem is that they’re solving. I must still be missing something.

It seems to me this topic of reproducible results with mirai would benefit from additional documentation. Maybe even a vignette of its own. What do you think? I could draft something into a PR if that would be helpful.

For context, here’s what I went through:

In my simulation code I always set the seed just before generating random numbers, like so:

``` r
set.seed(42)
lapply(1:2, function(i) runif(3))
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 0.9148060 0.9370754 0.2861395
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] 0.8304476 0.6417455 0.5190959
```

When converting sequential code to parallel with mirai, I usually just set the daemons up front. So my simulation code ended up looking like this:

``` r
library(mirai)

daemons(4)

set.seed(42)
mirai_map(1:2, function(i) runif(3))[]
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 0.5200912 0.8878523 0.2200554
#>

```

It took me a long time to figure out that I should actually be writing it like so:

``` r
``` r
library(mirai)

set.seed(42)

daemons(4)

#> [[1]]

However, I still don’t know when this is useful instead:

description:
I have a package A that internally uses `mirai_map()` in function `inner_loop`.

The problem is that this function might or might not be wrapped in another `mirai_map()` call by the user. That is, I need to structure my code that it works in three cases: 1) the user did not specify daemons, 2) the user called daemons, 3) the user used `mirai_map()` to call the function in parallel.

1 and 2 are working, but the nested mirai_maps calls I cannot get to work.
https://mirai.r-lib.org/articles/v01-map.html#nested-maps mentions that including a call to `daemons()` in the function provided to the outer map should work, but it does not work for me.

So besides a solution here, maybe it would be great to have a working sample in the vignettes (happy to write something up if I have a solution).

A simple MWE would be the following.

```R
# a function inside my package

  # setup the mirai cluster
  if (mirai::on_daemon()) {
    # call daemons to set deamons used by the inner loop
    # https://mirai.r-lib.org/articles/v01-map.html#nested-maps
    print("Connecting to existing Daemons!")
    # this is where the error lies

  } else if (mirai::status()$connections == 0) {
    # start daemons if not already running

    mirai::daemons(2)

title: Passing a custom TLS certificate in a `daemons()` call
description:
Currently both `daemons()` and `daemon()` share an argument `tls` that mean different things.

daemons(url = host_url(tls = TRUE), tls = tls)
launch_remote(n = 10, tls = tlscert, remote = cluster_config())

daemons(n = 10, url = host_url(tls = TRUE), tls = tls, tlscert = tlscert, remote = cluster_config())

title: daemon(dispatcher = TRUE) sets .Random.seed to NULL
description:
## Background

Plain R sessions (in the terminal, not an IDE like RStudio) begin without a `.Random.seed` object in the global environment.

```r
get(".Random.seed", envir = .GlobalEnv)
#> Error in get(".Random.seed", envir = .GlobalEnv) : 
#>   object '.Random.seed' not found
```

This is fine. However, once the RNG is invoked and `.Random.seed` exists, base R assumes it is always an integer. It is incorrect (or at least problematic) to manually set `.Random.seed` to `NULL`.

```r
sample.int(1L)
#> [1] 1

.Random.seed <- NULL

sample.int(1L)
#> [1] 1L
#> Warning message:
#> In sample.int(1L) :
#>   '.Random.seed' is not an integer vector but of type 'NULL', so ignored
```

This is different from removing the `.Random.seed` object from the global environment.

```r
sample.int(1L)
#> [1] 1

rm(.Random.seed, envir = .GlobalEnv)

sample.int(1L)
#> [1] 1L
```

But neither is ideal. Once `.Random.seed` is set, the correct way to reset the RNG state is `set.seed(seed = NULL)`.

## Issue

`mirai::daemon(dispatcher = TRUE)` sets `.Random.seed` to `NULL`, which causes the next downstream interaction with `.Random.seed` to throw a warning.

```r
mirai::daemons(n = 1L, url = "tcp://127.0.0.1:0", dispatcher = TRUE)
task <- mirai::mirai(TRUE)
url <- mirai::nextget("url")
mirai::daemon(url = url, maxtasks = 1L, cleanup = 0L, dispatcher = TRUE)
mirai::daemons(n = 0L)
set.seed(seed = NULL)
#>  Warning message:
#>  In set.seed(seed = NULL) :
#>    '.Random.seed' is not an integer vector but of type 'NULL', so ignored
```

The warning happens when `bundle[[1L]]` is `NULL`:

https://github.com/r-lib/mirai/blob/2ff1e10bd36891396a564500419d88eca93b9ebd/R/daemon.R#L130

If I modify this line to avoid setting `bundle[[1L]]` to `.Random.seed` when the value is `NULL`, then the warning is removed, both from this reprex and the current `crew` tests.

title: Make `everywhere()` using dispatcher robust to sending large data
description:
### Discussed in https://github.com/r-lib/mirai/discussions/281

Only an issue for dispatcher, as non-dispatcher uses a round-robin algorithm, so consecutive mirai are guaranteed to be sent to different daemons.

Current implementation for dispatcher relies on a [delay](https://github.com/r-lib/mirai/blob/main/R/mirai.R#L268) being added to the expression to temporarily block earlier daemons from attempting to evaluate an everywhere mirai meant for other daemons.

This is generally safe for initial setup use (as documented), but exporting large data could still be an edge case, as the time to serialize could mean that earlier mirai evaluations have completed by the time later ones are sent.

A more optimal, completely deterministic solution should be implemented.

#> [1] 2

What do you think about a function called `mirai_seed()` that:

title: Guard against recursive daemon spawning from mirai maps
description:
If a map function contains a local `daemons()` call then this can lead to an undesirable excessive number of running processes.

Note that this should not happen through package functions, as the guidance is specifically not for package authors to include `daemons()` calls, so would only (theoretically) apply to user-written functions.

If a map uses 8 daemons, and each then spawn 8 daemons, we now have 64 daemons.

On the other hand, it's safe to map to e.g. 8 processes locally, which then each map onto 8 daemons over the network, as the number of daemons would be controlled at 8 per machine.

So we need a way to prevent `daemons()` calls that create local daemons from within a `mirai_map()` call.

Note that by limiting the guard to local daemon creation, we offer an escape hatch as to get around this one could, instead of e.g. `daemons(6)`, use:

```r
daemons(url = local_url())
launch_local(6)
```

title: Mirai daemons persistence
description:
At the moment, the default behaviour is to let daemon processes end naturally and exit cleanly.

This means that daemons can outlive the host process, but only temporarily to finish any task that happens to be in progress. However, these tasks are not necessarily short-lived if, for example, some function causes the process to hang.

The callr package terminates child processes forcefully when the parent exits. This is also the default for crew, which wraps mirai.

It is likely safer for mirai to offer the same defaults.

title: Example of migrating ExtendedTask from future_promise to mirai
description:
I'm not sure if I use promises in a way that's unusual but I found migrating confusing as the slow function has to be included when the task is invoked rather than in the definition of the task. I got there eventually and wondered whether it would be helpful to include this example somewhere for others? Or is there another way to do it?

```
library(shiny)
library(bslib)
library(mirai)
library(promises)

future::plan(future::multisession)

# run app using 1 local daemon
daemons(1)

# automatically shutdown daemons when app exits
onStop(function() daemons(0))

ui <- page_fluid(
  p("The time is ", textOutput("current_time", inline = TRUE)),
  hr(),
  numericInput("n", "Sample size (n)", 100),
  numericInput("delay", "Seconds to take for plot", 5),
  input_task_button("m_btn", "Use mirai"),
  input_task_button("p_btn", "Use promises"),
  plotOutput("m_plot"),
  plotOutput("p_plot")

)

my_func <- function(x, y){
  Sys.sleep(y)
  runif(x)
}

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  output$current_time <- renderText({
    invalidateLater(1000)
    format(Sys.time(), "%H:%M:%S %p")
  })

  m_task <- ExtendedTask$new(
    function(run, ...) mirai(run(...), environment())
  ) |> bind_task_button("m_btn")

  p_task <- ExtendedTask$new(
    function(...) future_promise(my_func(...))
  ) |> bind_task_button("p_btn")

  observeEvent(input$m_btn, m_task$invoke(my_func, input$n, input$delay))
  observeEvent(input$p_btn, p_task$invoke(input$n, input$delay))

  output$m_plot <- renderPlot(hist(m_task$result()))
  output$p_plot <- renderPlot(hist(p_task$result()))

}

shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)
```

title: Modifying an R6 class from within `mirai` or `mirai_map`
description:
Hi @shikokuchuo, as requested, here's an attempt at a reprex regarding my issue mentioned over at [nanonext](https://github.com/r-lib/nanonext/discussions/109).

It is very simplified, but roughly shows my problem:

```R
Foo <- R6::R6Class(
    "Foo",
    public = list(

        ## FIELDS
        bar = NULL,

        ## METHODS
        iterate_sync = function() {
            purrr::map(1:5, \(i) self$bar[i] <- i)
            return(self$bar)
        },
        iterate_async = function() {
            with(
                mirai::daemons(4),
                mirai::mirai_map(1:5, \(i) self$bar[i] <- i)
            )
            return(self$bar)
        }
    )
)
```

Running the `iterate_sync` method gives:

```R
> foo <- Foo$new()
> foo$bar
NULL
> foo$iterate_sync()
[1] 1 2 3 4 5
> foo$bar
[1] 1 2 3 4 5
```

Whereas `iterate_async`:

```R
> foo <- Foo$new()
> foo$bar
NULL
> foo$iterate_async()
NULL
> foo$bar
NULL
```

Obviously this example is a bit silly since I can just run the map and assign to `self$bar` afterwards.

But my real case is more complicated and multiple fields are modified and so on, and if there is a simple fix to this that would be nice, to avoid a re-write. 

I am using Mirai elsewhere with success, by passing data via `.args` and/or `...`, but have not been able to get this case working.

title: Why does setting the seed in one `mirai_map()` use the same seed in another one?
description:
Hi, I came across some weird behavior related to randomness and I didn’t find related mentions in the docs (I looked for “random” and “seed”). In the example below, it appears that setting the seed in a `mirai_map()` keeps using the same seed in subsequent `mirai_map()` calls (the random draw is different across `mirai_map()` calls, but in a single `mirai_map()` the same seed is used everywhere).

``` r
library(mirai)
library(parallel)
packageVersion("mirai")
#> [1] '2.2.0.9001'

cl <- make_cluster(4)
daemons(4)
#> [1] 4
vec <- 1:3
vec2 <- 4:6

# Returns different values: good
mirai_map(list(vec, vec2), \(x) rnorm(x))[]
#> [[1]]
#> [1]  0.07040429  0.40971925 -0.39779374
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] -0.5323828  0.1015743 -0.5020980

# Set the seed in the function
mirai_map(list(vec, vec2), \(x) {
  set.seed(123)
  rnorm(x)
})[]
#> [[1]]
#> [1] -0.9685927  0.7061091  1.4890213
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] -0.9685927  0.7061091  1.4890213

# Do not set the seed in the function: still identical results?
mirai_map(list(vec, vec2), \(x) rnorm(x))[]
#> [[1]]
#> [1] -1.8150926  0.3304096 -1.1421557
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] -1.8150926  0.3304096 -1.1421557
```

Maybe I come with the wrong priors but I though that “what happens in the `mirai_map()` stays in the `mirai_map()`” and doesn’t contaminate others. I see that setting `dispatcher = FALSE` in `daemons()` solves this:

``` r
daemons(0)
#> [1] 0
daemons(4, dispatcher = FALSE)
#> [1] 4

mirai_map(list(vec, vec2), \(x) {
  set.seed(123)
  rnorm(x)
})[]
#> [[1]]
#> [1] -0.9685927  0.7061091  1.4890213
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] -0.9685927  0.7061091  1.4890213

mirai_map(list(vec, vec2), \(x) rnorm(x))[]
#> [[1]]
#> [1] -1.7628219  0.1110283  0.3758775
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1]  0.1192312 -0.4474403 -1.9538161
```

Should this be mentioned more prominently in the docs (unless I missed it)?

In any case, thanks for this package!

title: Understanding of nested mirai calls
description:
Hi Charlie,
thank you for the wonderful package.
I was wondering how the following code is supposed to work.
My use case is that I have an internal package that uses `mirai_map()` for parallelization and a shiny frontend which uses `mirai()` with ExtendedTask to not block the session.
I use `daemons()` only in the shiny server but I found that only the outer `mirai` call is parallelized, whereas the inner `mirai_map` is not running on the cluster.

A MWE looks like this:

```R
mirai::daemons(0)
paste("Hi from PID", Sys.getpid())
#> [1] "Hi from PID 718660"

tictoc::tic()
rr <- mirai::mirai({
  x <- paste("Hi from PID", Sys.getpid())
  
  res <- mirai::mirai_map(seq(4), function(i) {
    Sys.sleep(3)
    paste("Hi from PID", Sys.getpid(), "and i =", i)
  })
  
  c(x, res[])
})

rr[] |> unlist() |> paste(collapse = "\n") |> cat()
#> Hi from PID 721311
#> Hi from PID 721364 and i = 1
#> Hi from PID 721364 and i = 2
#> Hi from PID 721364 and i = 3
#> Hi from PID 721364 and i = 4

tictoc::toc()
#> 12.2 sec elapsed
```


Using 4 cores, I would expect to see different PIDs for each mirai_map call, as well as a full runtime of 3 seconds (maybe 6 seconds as one thread is occupied by the outer mirai call.

```R
mirai::daemons(4)
tictoc::tic()
paste("Hi from PID", Sys.getpid())
#> [1] "Hi from PID 718660"

rr <- mirai::mirai({
  x <- paste("Hi from PID", Sys.getpid())
  
  res <- mirai::mirai_map(seq(4), function(i) {
    Sys.sleep(3)
    paste("Hi from PID", Sys.getpid(), "and i =", i)
  })
  
  c(x, res[])
})

rr[] |> unlist() |> paste(collapse = "\n") |> cat()
#> Hi from PID 721668
#> Hi from PID 721876 and i = 1
#> Hi from PID 721876 and i = 2
#> Hi from PID 721876 and i = 3
#> Hi from PID 721876 and i = 4
tictoc::toc()
#> 12.2 sec elapsed
```

I see no speedup and that the mirai_map calls are all on the same PID.

title: stop_mirai() Not Stopping Downloads on Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS with ExtendedTask
description:
**Description**
I am experiencing an issue where the stop_mirai() function does not terminate the download process when running my Shiny app on Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS. Interestingly, the same code works as expected on Windows 11. I suspect that this might be related either to the way I am using mirai together with the ExtendedTask feature of Shiny, or it might be an underlying bug in mirai itself. My current suspicion is that the command on line 68 (stop_mirai(mirai_instance)) may not be resolving correctly due to how the mirai instance is defined in line 40 within the ExtendedTask definition.

**Steps to Reproduce**
- Use the minimal reproducible example provided below.
- Run the Shiny app on Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS.
- Click the Start Task button to initiate the download process.
- Click the Cancel Task button, which triggers stop_mirai(mirai_instance).
- Observe that the download process continues instead of stopping.

**Expected Behavior**
Clicking the Cancel Task button should trigger stop_mirai(mirai_instance), which in turn should halt the ongoing download process.

**Actual Behavior**
On Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS using RStudio Server, the download process does not stop when stop_mirai(mirai_instance) is called, despite the same code functioning correctly under Windows 11.

**Minimal Reproducible Example**
```
# app.R - Minimal reproducible example using ExtendedTask and mirai

# Packages ----------------------------------------------------------------
library(shiny)
library(shinyjs)
library(promises)   
library(bslib)   
library(mirai)      

BASE_PATH <- getwd()
output_path <- file.path(BASE_PATH, "output")
if (!dir.exists(output_path)) { dir.create(output_path) }

ui <- fluidPage(
  useShinyjs(),
  titlePanel("Minimal Extended Task Example"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      actionButton("start", "Start Task"),
      actionButton("cancel", "Cancel Task"),
      br(), br(),
      uiOutput("progress_ui")
    ),
    mainPanel(
      verbatimTextOutput("status")
    )
  )
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  
  mirai_instance <- reactiveVal(NULL) 
  
  files_to_download <- list(
    "https://nbg1-speed.hetzner.com/100MB.bin",
    "https://nbg1-speed.hetzner.com/100MB.bin",
    "https://nbg1-speed.hetzner.com/100MB.bin",
    "https://nbg1-speed.hetzner.com/100MB.bin"
  )
  
  extTask <- ExtendedTask$new(function(task_data) {
    mirai_instance <<- mirai(
      .args = list(
        files_to_download = task_data$files_to_download,
        output_path = task_data$output_path
      ),
      {
        local_files <- list()
        total <- length(files_to_download)
        for (i in seq_along(files_to_download)) {
          url        <- files_to_download[[i]]
          file_name  <- basename(url)
          local_file <- file.path(output_path, paste0(file_name, "_", i))
          if (!file.exists(local_file)) {
            curl::curl_download(url, destfile = local_file, mode = "wb")
          }
          local_files[[i]] <- local_file
        }
        local_files
      }
    )
  }) |> bind_task_button("start")
  
  observeEvent(input$start, {
    task_data <- list(files_to_download = files_to_download, output_path = output_path)
    extTask$invoke(task_data)
  })
  
  observeEvent(input$cancel, {
    stop_mirai(mirai_instance)
  })
  
  output$status <- renderPrint({
    req(extTask$result())
    extTask$result()
  })
}

daemons(1)
onStop(function() daemons(0))
shinyApp(ui, server)
```

**Environment Details**
- R version: 4.4.2 (2024-10-31)
- mirai Package Version: 2.2.0
- Other Relevant Package Versions: shiny (1.9.1), shinyjs (2.1.0), promises (1.3.0), bslib (0.8.0)
- RStudio Server Version: 2024.09.1 Build 394, "Cranberry Hibiscus" Release (a1fe401f, 2024-11-03) for Ubuntu Focal

Thank you for developing and maintaining the mirai package. I really appreciate the work put into this tool, as it has been incredibly useful for my projects. I look forward to your guidance and any fixes or suggestions you might have regarding this issue. Thanks again for your time and support!

title: Errors from `daemons()` specifying 'remote' leave daemons created
description:
As an example:

```r
> daemons(url = "tcp://127.0.0.1", remote = cfg)
Error in daemons(url = "tcp://127.0.0.1", remote = cfg) : 
  argument "n" is missing, with no default
```

The expectation would be that the operation failed.

But in fact it partially succeeded, as retrying by correctly specifying `n` then results in:

```r
> daemons(n = 1, url = "tcp://127.0.0.1", remote = cfg)
Error in daemons(n = 1, url = "tcp://127.0.0.1", remote = cfg) : 
  daemons already set for `default` compute profile
```
A failure should simply be a failure and not set up the daemons.

title: Running identical code multiple times has some `UnresolvedValue` results
description:
Hello, I've been continuing my experimentation with `mirai` and `shiny::ExtendedTask`. I'm encountering a large number of `UnresolvedValue` results and I'm unsure how to interpret this. I have some long running code that exists in an `R6` class. I create a new extended task and pass in the `R6` class; then when I invoke the extended task gets triggered and the code within the `R6` class gets called to return a new object.

I have a `shiny::bindEvent` that requires the `status` of the extended task to change to either `error` or `success` before continuing a `shiny::obseve` that takes the `result` of the extended task and either handles an error or continues with the app functionality.

This now works fine . . . the majority of the time. But a still relatively large proportion of times I receive an `UnresolvedValue` instead of the new object that I would expect from a `success` result. I've used `browser` to check and when this is happening the extended task has definitely reported a successful completion rather than an `error`.

So I'm trying to understand what situations will return an `UnresolvedValue` from a `mirai` that hasn't obviously had an error? Or how does the `mirai` interact with the `success` status from an `ExtendedTask`?

title: Inconsistent behaviour when creating a promise from a resolved mirai
description:
It is almost always the case that a promise is created before a mirai has resolved. However, it should resolve / reject in exactly the same way whether or not this is so.

Current code branch for already resolved promises leads to Shiny deep stack traces failing when the mirai returns an error i.e. either a `miraiError` or `errorValue`. This is rarely going to be the case as noted above, but should nevertheless be fixed.

The solution is to call `stop()` from the `resolve()` rather than rejecting directly. This simply mirrors the non-resolved branch.

title: unresolved() and data
description:
This topic has been low on my priority list until now, and it is by no means urgent, but I would like to discuss.

`crew` keeps the `mirai` objects of all the current tasks, and it needs to know which tasks are complete in order to do auto-scaling. To make decisions about when to launch new workers, `crew` compares the number of active workers to the number of incomplete tasks. To count the number of incomplete tasks, I cannot use counters `tasks_assigned` or `tasks_complete` because they only count tasks that have been assigned to a worker (ignoring the unassigned backlog) and because they reset every time a new worker connects to the socket. So instead, `crew` calls `unresolved()` on each `mirai()` object in the task list before making a decision about how many workers to launch. These launching decisions happen frequently (every `push()` and `pop()`, as well as every fraction of a second in `wait()`), so I would strongly prefer `unresolved()` to be fast.

As you explained in an earlier thread, `unresolved()` downloads the data in order to check if the task is complete. For most cases this may not be much of an issue, but for large enough data, this could slow down `crew` because of what needs to happen for auto-scaling. Also, it risks running into a situation where we have large objects from multiple tasks simultaneously in memory, and memory may not be adequate to store everything in a single session.

Would it be possible to allow `unresolved()` to avoid downloading the data so it can be fast and lightweight for medium to large data? Here is what I see with `mirai` 0.8.1:

```r
library(mirai)
library(lobstr)
daemons(n = 1L, url = "ws://127.0.0.1:5001", dispatcher = TRUE)
#> [1] 1
server <- callr::r_bg(function() mirai::server("ws://127.0.0.1:5001"))
daemons()
#> $connections
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $daemons
#> status_online status_busy tasks_assigned tasks_complete instance #
#> ws://127.0.0.1:5001             1           0              0              0          1
m <- mirai(rnorm(1e8))
Sys.sleep(10)
obj_size(m)
#> 6.01 kB
system.time(available <- !unresolved(m))
#> user  system elapsed 
#> 1.572   0.500   2.078
available
#> [1] TRUE
obj_size(m)
#> 800.01 MB
system.time(unresolved(m))
#> user  system elapsed 
#> 0       0       0
system.time(size <- obj_size(m$data))
#> user  system elapsed 
#> 0       0       0 
size
#> 800.00 MB
daemons(n = 0L)
#> [1] 0
server$kill()
```

title: WISH: Support passing name-value pairs via '.args' of mirai()
description:
Picking up on the side-discussion on argument `.args` that started in <https://github.com/shikokuchuo/mirai/issues/49#issuecomment-1497815283>.

As it stands now (mirai 0.8.2.9036), the `.args` argument of `mirai()` takes a vector of symbols as input.  The following are all working examples:

```r
m <- mirai::mirai(2 * a + b, .args = list(a, b))
m$data
## [1] 10
```

```r
m <- mirai::mirai(2 * a + b, .args = c(a, b))
m$data
## [1] 10
```

```r
m <- mirai::mirai(2 * a + b, .args = data.frame(a, b))
m$data
## [1] 10
```


# Issues

## Too broad acceptance

`?mirai::mirai` says that `.args` takes an "(optional) list of objects".  The above `.args = c(a, b)` example does not use a list.  One can also debate whether `.args = data.frame(a, b)` should work (although technically it's also a list).


## No validation of '.args'

There is no up-front validation of what is passed to `.args`.  Instead, mis-specification of `.args` results in run-time errors from worker failing to evaluate the expression.  For example,

```r
m <- mirai::mirai(2 * a + b, .args = c("a", "b"))
m$data
## 'miraiError' chr Error in 2 * a: non-numeric argument to binary operator
```

```r
m <- mirai::mirai(2 * a + b, .args = alist(a, b))
m$data
## 'miraiError' chr Error in 2 * a: non-numeric argument to binary operator
```

```r
m <- mirai::mirai(2 * a + b, .args = 42)
m$data
'miraiError' chr Error in eval(expr = envir[[".expr"]], envir = envir, enclos = NULL): object 'a' not found
```


## No support for name-value pairs

I think there will be a lot of users that will expect being able to do:

```r
m <- mirai::mirai(2 * a + b, .args = list(a = 3, b = 4))
m$data
'miraiError' chr Error in eval(expr = envir[[".expr"]], envir = envir, enclos = NULL): object 'a' not found
```

This will allow users to write more clear code.  Currently, anyone who wishes to pass a named list of values has to resort to `do.call()`, which counter to the "neat API" that **mirai** tries to support.  For example, as it stands now, we have to write code like:

```r
expr <- quote(2 * a + b)
globals <- list(a = 3, b = 4)
m <- do.call(mirai, c(list(expr), globals))
```

instead of a much cleaner and less obscure:

```r
expr <- quote(2 * a + b)
globals <- list(a = 3, b = 4)
m <- mirai(expr, .args = globals)
```


# Suggestion

1. Redesign current behavior to support only the `.args = c(a, b)` form.

2. Add support for specifying name-value elements, i.e. `.args = list(a = 3, b = 4)`.

I think those will be the most common use cases. Using `c()` for one and `list()` for the other could help distinguish the two.  Of course, both forms could be handled using `list()` too.

FWIW, the fact that `c(a, b)` uses symbols has the advantage that static-code inspection (e.g. **codetools** validation by `R CMD check`) can pick up typos.  In contrast, `.args = c("a", "btypo")` won't be detected until run-time.

title: WISH: Pass an expression to '.expr' as-is to mirai()
description:
Consider the following example:

```r
a <- 3
b <- 4
m <- mirai(2 * a + b, .args = list(a, b))
```


# Issue

Now, assume that I have that R expression and a list of variables as standalone objects, e.g.

```r
.expr <- quote(2 * a + b)
a <- 3
b <- 4
globals <- list(a = a, b = b)
```

To use this setup with `mirai()`, I need to do something like:

```r
.expr2 <- bquote({
  local({
    envir <- parent.env(environment())
    for (name in names(globals)) {
      assign(name, value = globals[[name]], envir = envir)
    }
  })
  .(.expr)
})

call_expr <- bquote(mirai(.(.expr2), .args = list(globals)))
m <- eval(call_expr)
```


# Wish

If there would be an option to _not_ `substitute()` the `.expr` argument, then I could instead do:

```r
m <- do.call(mirai, args = c(list(.expr), globals, .substitute = FALSE))
```

title: experimental thread dispatcher for daemons sometimes fails to reach everywhere
description:
I'd previously reported a bug in `daemons()` when using the dispatcher. I initially thought it was a problem elsewhere, so the first report was moved to a [discussion topic](https://github.com/shikokuchuo/mirai/issues/132) after some back and forth without being addressed. A [second attempt](https://github.com/shikokuchuo/mirai/issues/132) was fixed in a subsequent release and has been working. I've now discovered a similar bug in the newer experimental `"thread"` dispatcher option. In my local experiments, it doesn't always manifest (e..g., if the daemon count is only 1 or 2), but the example below should readily summon the defect when using a daemon count of 5 or greater.

Once again, I'm not at liberty to show what I'm really doing, so I've made a rather silly and chatty reprex for you using the [lgr](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/lgr/) package from Stefan Fleck. This code provisions a few daemons, loads the lgr package on them with `everywhere()`, and then configures the root logger on them using `everywhere()`.  The code continues from there using mirai's future-promise approach to produce log events using the deamon logger reference that was captured during the logger's configuration (all local to each daemon). I force the resolution of all those mirai objects and then inspect the full set of them looking for any that could/did not complete. The daemons are then torn down. This full process will cycle repeatedly. The example should reproduce the issue almost immediately and, through inspection, you can see that some daemons don't have that logger reference and thus throw errors.

```
# reprex for thread dispatcher issue
library(mirai)
cnt <- 1L
while (TRUE) {
  mirai::daemons(n = 5, dispatcher = "thread")
  mirai::everywhere(library(lgr))
  mirai::everywhere(.expr = {lg <<- lgr::basic_config(threshold = "all", console = "info")})
  m.vec <- unlist(lapply(1:1000, FUN = function(i) {
    m <- mirai::mirai(lg$info("log blather... <sigh>"))
    resolved.mirai <- call_mirai_(m)
    return(resolved.mirai$data)
  }))
  not.really.resolved.mirai.cnt <- sum(grepl(pattern = "Error*", m.vec))
  if (not.really.resolved.mirai.cnt > 0) {
    message("I'm not reproducible on run #", cnt, " because "
            , not.really.resolved.mirai.cnt
            , " time(s) out of 1000 I was not really ready :'-(")
  }
  daemons(0)

} 
```

title: Support for mirai cancellation
description:
Hi Charlie, while it was on my mind, I just wanted to jot down some thoughts regarding cancellation, in case it's a feature you're ever interested in pursuing (which would definitely be great for Shiny btw). Probably a lot of the below is not news to you, hope I don't offend you by stating what might be obvious to you--these are just my thoughts.

There are several parts to cancellation: 1) how you invoke it, 2) how it cancels the task, 3) how/when it's reported back to the controlling process.

## Invocation

The obvious would be `mirai$cancel()`. The alternative is to use a [cancellation token](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.cancellationtoken?view=net-8.0), where each mirai needs to be handed a cancellation-signaling object during construction. For starting/cancelling a single task, the cancel() method is easier; but for coordinating lots of tasks that are logically part of a single operation, the cancellation token approach is easier.

It might be more convenient to have `with(cancellationToken, { ... })`, i.e. the ability to install a default global cancellation token.

## Cancellation

It's either cooperative (make the user's mirai expression explicitly check for interruption) or non-cooperative (send SIGINT/Ctrl+C). For R, probably the vast majority of the time, non-cooperative is fine? But it seems wrong not to make cooperative possible (or at least the ability for the user to say "during this critical section, don't let me be interrupted").

I guess the "pick reasonable defaults" approach would be for it to be non-cooperative by default and then have a way to override the default behavior to ask for cooperative instead. While the "be explicit" approach would be to not support cancellation unless the `mirai()` function is explicitly told whether the code is designed for cooperative cancellation, or ready for non-cooperative interruption.

## Reporting back

Cancellation could be fire-and-forget (the mirai object acts as if interruption succeeded immediately, even if the task is still actually running), like posix signals.

Or it could join on the task, so the user can know whether it was actually interrupted or if it ran to completion before it had a chance to be interrupted. You could imagine the latter distinction mattering for side-effecty operations--like if you tried to cancel a bank transfer, it's important to know whether the cancellation succeeded. I personally have found in practice this seems to almost never matter--or at least, it's nice to know if the task has actually stopped but the distinction between "it stopped because you asked it to" vs. "it stopped on its own" rarely matters; in the bank transfer example you'd probably want to do a query to determine whether it succeeded or not, anyway.

_Originally posted by @cdriveraus in https://github.com/shikokuchuo/mirai/issues/137#issuecomment-2309592791_
            
Separating out this issue as I'm not sure it belongs with general guidance for using `mirai` within a package.

The behaviour for `everywhere()` is everywhere _for a specific compute profile_ - it was never across all compute profiles. In this way, as it's designed to be called for setup rather than continually, it probably doesn't matter so much if the '.compute' argument is vectorised or not - you can just call it multiple times.

This is related to the design in general of `mirai` not to throw errors when not necessary, returning 'errorValues' instead for example. However in this case, it probably makes sense for more explicit behaviour here.

title: everywhere() sometimes fails to reach everywhere when using dispatcher
description:
I'd previously tried to substantiate the case that there is an issue here to no avail. You can read more in my [last comment on my previous issue that was downgraded to the discussion forum](https://github.com/shikokuchuo/mirai/discussions/131#discussioncomment-10153919). It has more details and commentary along with a slightly different example.

It is clear to me that `everywhere()` is not reliable for reproducible work when placed under even moderate load. Using the same example code supplied in the documentation, you can readily break the behavior by exerting a bit of pressure. In the example code, the `parallel` package that is included in the base R distribution is loaded and attached to the search path via the call `everywhere(library(parallel))`. Subsequently, a `mirai("package:parallel" %in% search())` call is made and that mirai is resolved with a call to `call_mirai()`. That may work well on the single daemon that was started; however, try expanding that example to execute many times across a larger set of daemons and witness intermittent failures over iterations of that process:

```{r}
library(mirai)
cnt <- 1L
while (TRUE) {
  daemons(10)
  everywhere(library(parallel))
  m.vec <- unlist(lapply(1:1000, FUN = function(i) {
    m <- mirai("package:parallel" %in% search())
    resolved.mirai <- call_mirai_(m)
    return(resolved.mirai$data)
  }))
  not.really.resolved.mirai.cnt <- sum(!m.vec)
  if (not.really.resolved.mirai.cnt > 0) {
    message("I'm not reproducible on run #", cnt, " because "
            , not.really.resolved.mirai.cnt
            , " time(s) out of 1000 I was not really ready :'-(")
  }
  daemons(0)
  cnt <- cnt + 1L
} 
```

Be patient as it may take a few tries, but eventually you'll see failures. Here are some of my own:

```
I'm not reproducible on run #8 because 126 time(s) out of 1000 I was not really ready :'-(
I'm not reproducible on run #26 because 316 time(s) out of 1000 I was not really ready :'-(
I'm not reproducible on run #50 because 46 time(s) out of 1000 I was not really ready :'-(

I'm not reproducible on run #80 because 380 time(s) out of 1000 I was not really ready :'-(
I'm not reproducible on run #85 because 571 time(s) out of 1000 I was not really ready :'-(
```

To me, what I'm doing above is not an unreasonable extension to the example that was supplied to test the behavior _under pressure_ which is how all production work should be evaluated. Per my [last comment in the previous issue I tried to open](https://github.com/shikokuchuo/mirai/discussions/131#discussioncomment-10153919), this is either a bug in the code or a bug in the documentation because the function does not do what it claims to do. You might think this is an artifact of the pressure exerted here of pushing a 1000 mirai onto 10 daemons, but that's not the case. If you reduce the `lapply()` to only `10` iterations to match the daemon count, it will still fail intermittently -- you'll just need to be more patient since it becomes less likely to happen.

As it is, users should be prepared for unexpected failures in scripts for any non-trivial setup work at scale.

title: How to know when everywhere() is done with everything
description:
I'm still thoroughly appreciating this excellent package. Thank you! This is the best thing that has happened to R in several years. 

I'm working on an application that needs to process ~850 requests/minute. I've historically used stable persistent clusters (leveraging `parallel` and `parallelly`), but I wanted to migrate it to your lovely package since the polling in my previous setup was creating a rather heavy parallel 'tax'. I was noticing some very odd intermittent failures in my set of provisioning functions that ensure all workers are loaded with packages and variables as well as my own parallel logger routines. It seemed at times that `everywhere()` might be failing. I threw some breakpoints in my package and rebuilt and, sure enough, caught what seems to be intermittent points where previous steps of provisioning are not completed even though `everywhere()` had been called. Rerunning those lines while in the debugger allowed me continue on.

On one hand, this makes sense; a `mirai` is an async future. But how does one check on a call to `everywhere()` other than to inspect the `search()` path, `.GlobalEnv`, etc. (depending on what I've done) of each worker since the function has no return value? It took a minute before I resorted to some code violence.

Being the gangstR that I am, I decided some good old fashioned torture might get it talk to me. The reprex below will provision 10 `daemons()`. Once it makes sure they're connected, I set a `node.pid` value in each `daemon` and then try to retrieve them all by calling an excessive amount of `mirai()` (knowing that there is no reason to expect a uniform set of returns, I can imagine some will be missing from time to time). Because we know those will take time, I add a delay (with exponential backoff). To test whether `everywhere()` also has an effect, too, I place an earlier delay before the set of `mirai` are called.  Once all `node.pid` values are recovered from the `daemons`, I reset them and start the provisioning over again and again.

```{r}
library(mirai)

node.cnt <- 10

while (TRUE) {
  daemons(node.cnt)
  
  count <- 0L
  while (TRUE) {
    count <- count + 1L
    out <- daemons()$daemons
    if (is.matrix(out)) {
      break
    }
  }
  message("Daemons ready after ", count, " status check(s)")
  
  count <- 0L
  while (TRUE) {
    everywhere(node.pid <<- Sys.getpid())
    Sys.sleep(2^count)  # Something strange is afoot at the Circle K if you remove this
    m <- lapply(1:1000, FUN = function(x) {mirai(print(node.pid))})
    Sys.sleep(2^count)  # We expect to either wait here or else call in the mirai resolution...
    pid.vec <- unique(na.omit(unlist(lapply(m, FUN = function(x) {x$data}))))
    pid.df <- data.frame(pid = pid.vec, id = order(pid.vec))
    count <- count + 1L
    if (nrow(pid.df) == node.cnt) {
      break
    } else {
      message("...only ", nrow(pid.df), " row(s) present but expected ", node.cnt)
    }
  }
  message("All nodes replying after ", count, " status check(s)\n\n")
  
  daemons(0)
}
```

Here's a short sample run:
```
Daemons ready after 1 status check(s)
All nodes replying after 1 status check(s)


Daemons ready after 1 status check(s)
...only 9 row(s) present but expected 10
All nodes replying after 2 status check(s)


Daemons ready after 1 status check(s)
...only 8 row(s) present but expected 10
All nodes replying after 2 status check(s)


Daemons ready after 1 status check(s)
...only 9 row(s) present but expected 10
All nodes replying after 2 status check(s)
```

What's interesting is that I notice that commenting out the first delay (after the `everywhere()`) has quite a noticeable effect on the progress (i.e., _it gets much worse_). This shows up as:

```
Daemons ready after 1 status check(s)
...only 0 row(s) present but expected 10
All nodes replying after 2 status check(s)


Daemons ready after 1 status check(s)
...only 0 row(s) present but expected 10
All nodes replying after 2 status check(s)


Daemons ready after 1 status check(s)
...only 0 row(s) present but expected 10
All nodes replying after 2 status check(s)


Daemons ready after 1 status check(s)
...only 0 row(s) present but expected 10
...only 9 row(s) present but expected 10
All nodes replying after 3 status check(s)


Daemons ready after 1 status check(s)
...only 7 row(s) present but expected 10
All nodes replying after 2 status check(s)
```

I repeated this behavior many times (commenting and uncommenting the first delay). This seems to suggest that I should devise checks after my calls to `everywhere()` to make sure that the provisioning work has completed. Or is there simply a way to block and wait for them to complete as there is with `mirai`? Keep in mind, my applications run on Linux but these tests were ran on a very modest Windows laptop; thus, not particularly fast.

One other minor/unrelated question: Is there a way to get the `i` value from a `daemon` (that shows in `status()`) to know its identity as part of a `mirai`? It will be handy to know which worker processed my future in a less convoluted way than I've devised locally. Thank you

title: mirai don't start with custom .libPaths nor options
description:
I don't know whether this is really a bug, or maybe you envision mirai's task to start on vanilla R session not inheriting any information from parent session (where it is invoked from). In my case I have an .Rprofile file and .Renviron file in a "project" directory and my "parent session" includes custom options and custom .libPaths(). `mirai` seem to start an R session in system default directory.

 
Let's imagine you have some `options()` and `.libPaths()` changed through `.Rprofile`

### failing solution
```r
.libPaths("~/new_dir")
options(repos = c(myrepo = "myrepo.mydomain"))
run_fun <- function() {
  list(
    repos = options()$repos,
    libpaths = .libPaths()
  )    
}

task1 <- mirai::mirai(run(), run = run_fun)
identical(task1$data, run_fun())
# FALSE
```

### working solution

I'm forced to set the process in a way where I set `options` and `.libPaths` through the `args`. 

```r
.libPaths("~/new_dir")
options(repos = c(myrepo = "myrepo.mydomain"))
run_fun_with_opts <- function(opts, libpaths) {
  options(opts)
  .libPaths(libpaths)
  list(
    repos = options()$repos,
    libpaths = .libPaths()
  )
}
task2 <- mirai::mirai(run(opts, libpaths), run = run_fun_with_opts, opts = options(), libpaths = .libPaths())
identical(task2$data, run_fun())
# TRUE
```

--------

I think it makes sense to start an R process by default from the same directory as working directory (to include `.Rprofile` or `.Renviron`). Only `options` or system vars set outside of the `.Rprofile` and `.Renviron` should be handled by the user. What is your opinion about this?

title: Support manual task retries?
description:
Previously, the dispatcher automatically retried tasks which did not get a chance to finish. https://github.com/shikokuchuo/mirai/commit/6a72261f070bbada0be872bda4d66383addcb58c removes this feature and causes these tasks to return with an "error 19" code. 

Without automatic retries, the dispatcher does not have to hold on to data from unresolved tasks, so I can see how this would increase memory efficiency. However, it is a setback for {crew} because there is no longer a way to recover from crashed workers. Workers can crash for perfectly normal and expected reasons: for example, if a spike in spot instance pricing causes an AWS Batch worker to exit. We want to retry the task in those cases.

Would it be possible to manually retry a `mirai` object? If so, `crew` would be able to easily resubmit the task when it tries to collect the result and instead gets the "error 19" code. It might also be good to take this opportunity to limit the number of retries for a task, so keeping track of the number of tries for each task would also be valuable.
